title: Scenario-engine release Pods stuck Pending
telemetry: Supplied sanitized GKE console observations: Workloads Deployment and Pod event views, node pool details, Logs Explorer cluster autoscaler visibility entries (k8s_cluster), Compute Engine managed instance group views and the Quotas page, plus the application owner's release record. Static console-observation profile with no kubectl, gcloud, cluster credentials or node access. The example GKE version is a synthetic snapshot and makes no current-support claim.
owner: Ximena, Market Stress on-call, owns the investigation; Kofi, the scenario-engine application and release owner, owns its Pod template, resource requests and the 6.2.0 rollout; Annika, the GKE platform owner, owns stress-compute's node pools, machine types and autoscaling limits; Ravi, the cloud quota and policy owner, owns project quotas, quota requests and organization policy. ITO coordinates the existing TLC and change approvals.
task: Ximena has asked you to investigate why the scenario-engine 6.2.0 rollout in GKE cluster stress-compute, namespace market-stress, project synthetic-stress-prod, us-east1, has Pods stuck Pending. Review the supplied console observations for 2026-10-14 10:00-10:40 UTC and return a bounded technical finding for the existing TLC: whether the workload's configuration or the cluster's ability to add capacity blocks scheduling, the evidence, remaining unknowns, and the next useful check with its owner. No change is approved.

sources.claim: The scheduler places a Pod only where the sum of requests fits node capacity, regardless of actual usage; an unschedulable Pod stays unscheduled with a FailedScheduling event (the page's example reads '0/42 nodes available: insufficient cpu'). Remedies include adding nodes, freeing room, and checking that the Pod is not larger than all the nodes. The fixture's exact scheduler wording is not graded.

maxSurge and maxUnavailable bound Pods above desired and unavailable during a rolling update, and they cannot both be 0; progressDeadlineSeconds defaults to 600, after which the Deployment reports Progressing=False with reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded. Kubernetes takes no other action on a stalled Deployment, so the old Pods keep serving and no automatic rollback occurs.

The cluster autoscaler works per node pool and decides from Pod resource requests, not utilization; --min-nodes/--max-nodes are per-zone limits. Scale-up can fail on node creation errors such as insufficient quota, and the autoscaler then backs off from five minutes up to 30 minutes.

Visibility events are in log container.googleapis.com/cluster-autoscaler-visibility, queried with resource.type k8s_cluster. scaleUp carries increasedMigs, requestedNodes and triggeringPods; eventResult follows a scaleUp and its errorMsg can be scale.up.error.quota.exceeded naming the failing groups; noScaleUp is best-effort, emitted every couple of minutes per persisting reason, with rejectedMigs reason no.scale.up.mig.failing.predicate (predicate name and reason, e.g. NodeResourcesFit), top-level no.scale.up.in.backoff and no.scale.up.nap.disabled. The page does not document an organization-policy scale-up error, so the case does not use one.

The autoscaler adds nodes to a pool only if its machine type provides enough resources; for no.scale.up.mig.failing.predicate review the Pod's requirements, and either correct inaccurate requests or create a node pool with a machine type that fits. scale.up.error.quota.exceeded means some groups could not grow due to Compute Engine quota, visible in the group's Errors tab, with a backoff of up to 30 minutes; the remedy is a quota increase, which here is an owner decision under approval.

CPU quota is regional and counts virtual CPUs across all VM instances in a region; N2 machine types use their own N2_CPUS pool, separate from the CPUS pool used by E2 and N1; resources cannot be created once the limit is reached. The page gives no exact error text, so the fixture's QUOTA_EXCEEDED Errors-tab summary is not graded for wording.

a.conclusion: Release 6.2.0 raised the scenario-engine CPU request from 5 to 10, more than the 8 CPU capacity of any n2-standard-8 node in scenario-pool, the only node pool. The scheduler finds no node and the autoscaler rejects both scenario-pool groups on NodeResourcesFit, with node auto-provisioning disabled, so adding nodes of this shape cannot place the Pods. Quota headroom and the unreached pool maximum rule out a capacity-provisioning block. The 6.1.3 Pods keep serving; whether the workload needs 10 CPU is unproven.
next_checks: Kofi, the application and release owner, confirms whether 6.2.0's cpu 10 request is intended and what the workload needs per Pod, comparing it with 6.1.3's cpu 5.

If the request is a mistake, Kofi proposes a corrected template under ITO's change approval; if 10 CPU is genuinely needed, Annika evaluates a node pool with a machine type that fits it as a platform change. Neither is authorized by this investigation.

Ximena tracks the stalled rollout and the 6.1.3 Pods' serving health in the existing TLC against the 12:00 UTC stress run, and decides with Kofi whether to pause or undo the rollout through the normal approval path.

b.conclusion: The 6.2.0 Pods request the same cpu 5 as 6.1.3 and would fit a new scenario-pool node, but the existing nodes are full. The cluster autoscaler tried three times to add three nodes, below the pool maximum, and each attempt failed on Compute Engine N2_CPUS quota in us-east1, which is fully used. Three replay-batch instances outside the cluster consume the headroom the pool used on 2026-10-13. The workload configuration is not the blocker; who owns the replay-batch instances and whether the quota should change is unproven.
